title: Even strong certainty keeps company with pious solicitude, not carnal security
source_text: XXXVI. In eo quoque consensus est, quantacunque sit illa fiducia & certitudo, ad quam omnes fideles eniti & contendere debent, & ad quam qui sunt inter eos perfectiores perveniunt, illam tamen non omnem timorem expellere, sed esse quendam timorem qui cum eo compatiatur, & qui debeat ejus esse perpetuus comes. Etenim hic distinguunt Protestantium Theologi inter timorem dubitationis, sive diffidentiae, & inter timorem piae sollicitudinis, qui securitati carnali opponitur, cum quo jubemur nostram salutem operari. Illum foras mittit charitas, ex qua fiducia apud Deum oritur, hic vero cum spe & fiducia firmissime stat & conciliatur.
pass_a_gloss: In this also there is consensus, that however great that trust and certainty may be toward which all the faithful ought to strive and contend, and to which those who are more perfect among them arrive, nevertheless it does not drive out every fear, but there is a certain fear which is compatible with it, and which ought to be its perpetual companion. For here the theologians of the Protestants distinguish between the fear of doubt, or of distrust, and the fear of pious solicitude, which is opposed to carnal security, with which we are commanded to work out our salvation. The former charity casts out, from which trust toward God arises; but the latter stands and is reconciled most firmly with hope and trust.
pass_b_english: Mature assurance still keeps a godly fear of solicitude.
Protestants cast out distrustful fear, not the watchful fear that wars against carnal security.
